title: River training works
summary: The reliable marks here are the spur orientation rule — a spur pointing UPSTREAM repels the flow away from the bank, one pointing downstream attracts it — and the guide bank scour multipliers on Lacey's normal depth. Understand why a river meanders and where it erodes (the concave outer bank, where the helical current scours) and most of the rest follows. For Nepal, gabions are the standard technique and the reasons are specifically local: local boulders, no cement, flexible, permeable, unskilled labour.

sections.heading: River behaviour and classification
sections.body:
**Why rivers are trained.** A natural alluvial river is **mobile**: it erodes one bank, deposits on the other, meanders, braids, and shifts its course over years. River training works impose enough stability for a structure or a settlement to survive beside it.

**Objectives of river training:**

| Objective | Means |
|---|---|
| **Protect banks and land** from erosion | Revetment, spurs, gabions |
| **Guide the flow** through a structure | Guide banks |
| **Confine the flood** within defined limits | Marginal embankments (levees) |
| **Improve the channel** for discharge or navigation | Dredging, cut-offs, closing bars |
| **Prevent shifting** of the course | Combination of the above |
| Provide depth at an intake | Spurs, dredging |

**Classification of rivers by reach**, from source to sea:

| Reach | Character |
|---|---|
| **Rocky / mountainous** | Steep, confined by rock, boulder bed; **little training possible or needed** |
| **Boulder (sub-mountainous)** | Steep, boulder and gravel bed, **braided**, wide shifting channel — **the Nepali hill and Bhabar rivers** |
| **Alluvial (flood plain)** | Gentle slope, sand bed, **meandering**; erodible banks — **the Terai rivers** |
| Deltaic / tidal | Very flat, distributaries, tidal influence |

**Nepal's rivers span the first three within a very short horizontal distance**, which is why river engineering there is distinctive: a river may fall from 3000 m to 100 m in under 100 km, changing from a rocky torrent to a braided boulder channel to a meandering sand-bed river. The training problem is therefore quite different at each reach, and a technique appropriate in the Terai may be useless in the hills.

**Classification by behaviour:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Straight** | Rare in nature over any length; sinuosity < 1.1 |
| **Meandering** | **Sinuosity > 1.5**; a single channel swinging in loops |
| **Braided** | Multiple interlacing channels around shifting bars; **heavy sediment load and steep slope** |
| Aggrading | **Bed rising** — sediment supply exceeds transport capacity |
| Degrading | **Bed falling** — transport capacity exceeds supply |
| Stable / in regime | Neither |

**Aggradation and degradation are the two conditions that defeat a structure**, and both are commonly triggered by human action:

| Cause | Effect |
|---|---|
| A **dam** upstream traps sediment | **Degradation** downstream — the "hungry water" erodes the bed, undermining bridges and intakes |
| **Deforestation or road construction** in the catchment | Increased sediment supply → **aggradation** downstream, raising flood levels |
| **Sand and gravel mining** from the bed | Local degradation, undermining structures |
| Channel straightening | Steeper slope → degradation |

That a dam causes **degradation downstream** while deforestation causes **aggradation** is worth holding as a pair, because both have caused documented damage in Nepal — the second more widely, as hill road construction has raised the sediment load of many Terai rivers and with it their flood levels.

**Meandering — the terms and the mechanism:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Meander length** | The distance along the axis for one complete loop |
| **Meander belt** | The width swept by the meanders |
| **Meander (loop) width** | — |
| **Sinuosity** | **Curved length ÷ straight (valley) length** |
| **Cut-off** | When a loop's neck is breached, the loop is abandoned |
| **Ox-bow lake** | The abandoned loop, left as a crescent lake |

**Why a river erodes the OUTER (concave) bank.** In a bend, the water surface superelevates toward the outside, and the resulting pressure gradient drives a **secondary (helical) current**: water flows **outward at the surface** and **inward along the bed**. The consequences follow directly:

| Bank | Process |
|---|---|
| **Concave (outer)** | **Scoured and deepened** — the surface current attacks it, and the bed load is swept away |
| **Convex (inner)** | **Silted** — the bed current carries sediment toward it, forming a **point bar** |

So the river **erodes the outside and deposits on the inside of every bend**, which is exactly why meanders **grow and migrate downstream** rather than staying put.

**Two practical consequences worth carrying:**

1. **An intake belongs on the concave (outer) bank**, where the water is **deep and relatively free of bed load** — a free advantage from the river's own hydraulics.
2. **Bank protection is needed on the concave bank**, and it must extend **downstream** of the point of maximum attack, because the attack point migrates.

sections.heading: Guide banks
sections.body:
**Guide banks (Bell's bunds)** confine and **guide the river through the waterway** of a bridge, barrage or weir, and prevent it outflanking the structure.

**Their purpose is precise:** a wide braided river approaching a structure of limited waterway must be **funnelled** into it, in a **stable, central and axial** flow, without attacking the abutments or the approach embankments. Guide banks do that.

**Layout:**

| Element | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Length upstream of the axis** | **1.0 to 1.25 L** (L = waterway length) |
| Length downstream | 0.2 to 0.4 L |
| **Upstream curved head** | A **circular curve of radius 0.4 to 0.5 L**, turning through 120–145° |
| Downstream curved head | Radius 0.3 to 0.5 of the upstream radius, turning through 45–60° |
| Top width | 6 – 9 m (often carries a service road) |
| Free board above HFL | 1.0 – 1.5 m |
| Side slope | 2:1 |

**The curved heads are the critical parts**, and their curvature is what makes the arrangement work: a straight-ended bank would present a blunt obstruction and generate severe local scour and eddies. The **curved head guides the flow smoothly** into the waterway, so the streamlines converge without separation.

**They are also where the deepest scour occurs**, and this is the most examined numerical item in the subchapter.

**Scour depth.** From **Lacey's normal scour depth**:

> **R = 0.473 (Q/f)^{1/3}**  for unrestricted width, or **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** per unit width

the **maximum anticipated scour** is a multiple of R:

| Location | Multiplier |
|---|---|
| **Straight reach of a guide bank** | **1.25 R** |
| **Nose (transition) of a guide bank** | **1.5 R** |
| **Upstream curved head (mole head)** | **2.0 to 2.75 R** |
| Downstream curved head | 1.5 R |
| Nose of a bridge pier | 2.0 R |
| Severe bend | 1.75 – 2.0 R |

**The upstream curved head takes the deepest scour** — up to about **2.75 times** the normal depth — because that is where the flow is turned most sharply and the local velocity and turbulence are greatest. Protection there must be correspondingly heavy, and it is the standard place for a guide bank to fail.

**Protection of a guide bank:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **Slope pitching (revetment)** | Stone, concrete blocks or gabions on the river-side slope, armouring it against the current |
| **Launching (falling) apron** | Loose stone laid on the bed at the toe, which **launches itself down the scour slope** as the bed erodes, forming a protective cover |
| **Filter layer** | Under the pitching, preventing the bank material being washed out through the joints |
| Toe wall | Anchors the base of the pitching |

**The launching apron is the elegant part of the design.** Rather than attempting to found the protection below the deepest anticipated scour — which would require enormous excavation under water — a **quantity of loose stone is laid on the bed** at the toe. As the bed scours, the stone **slides (launches) down the developing slope**, arriving as a continuous armour layer over the scoured face. The design therefore computes the **volume of stone required to cover the launched slope** (conventionally taken as **2:1**) to an adequate thickness, and lays that volume on the bed in advance.

> **Apron stone volume ≈ (launched slope length) × (launched thickness), with the launched thickness taken as about 1.25 times the laid thickness**

The stone size must resist the velocity — sized by **Neill's or Izbash's** criterion — and where individual stones are too small to be stable, they are **bound in wire crates (gabions)** or replaced by **concrete blocks**.

**Marginal embankments (levees)** are the other confinement work: earthen banks running **parallel to the river** at some distance, containing the flood within a defined flood plain. Their design points: adequate **free board**, **side slopes** stable under rapid drawdown, protection where the river approaches them, **borrow pits on the country side** (not the river side, where they would weaken the bank), and **sluices** to drain the country-side land whose natural outfall the embankment has blocked.

**The embankment's own hazard** deserves stating: by confining the flood, an embankment **raises the flood level** within the confined channel and **prevents sediment depositing on the flood plain**, so the **bed aggrades** and the level rises further over decades. The embankment must then be raised, and the process repeats. A breach then releases a far deeper flood than would have occurred naturally. This is the well-documented history of embanked rivers in the Indo-Gangetic plain, and it is why embankment is not an unqualified good.

sections.heading: Spurs, revetment and bank protection
sections.body:
**Spurs (groynes)** project from the bank into the river, and they work by **altering the flow pattern** rather than merely armouring the bank.

**The orientation rule — the most examined item in the subchapter:**

| Spur points | Called | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM** (inclined against the flow) | **REPELLING** | **Pushes the flow AWAY from the bank** |
| **DOWNSTREAM** (inclined with the flow) | **ATTRACTING** | **Draws the flow TOWARD the bank** |
| **Perpendicular** to the bank | **Deflecting** | Deflects locally without much repulsion |

**A repelling spur is the usual choice for bank protection**, because pushing the current away from the bank is the object. An **attracting** spur is used deliberately where the flow must be **brought toward** a bank — for example to maintain depth at an intake, or to hold the river against a hard bank and away from an erodible one.

**Typical orientation:** a repelling spur is set at about **60 to 75° to the bank, pointing upstream**.

**How spurs work beyond deflection.** A series of spurs creates **still-water pockets between them**, in which **sediment deposits**. Over a few flood seasons those pockets silt up and become vegetated, and the effective bank line moves out to the spur heads — so the spurs create a **new, protected bank** rather than merely defending the old one. That progressive siltation is why a spur field is often more durable than a continuous revetment, and cheaper per kilometre.

**Spacing** is typically **2 to 2.5 times the spur length** in a straight reach, closer on a concave bank and wider on a convex one. Too wide and the flow re-attacks the bank between them; too close and the cost rises without benefit.

**Types of spur:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Impermeable (solid)** | Earth core with stone or gabion armour; **deflects** the flow |
| **Permeable (screen, pile)** | Piles, timber or bamboo screens; **slows** the flow and **induces siltation** rather than deflecting it |
| **T-headed** | A head at right angles, giving better protection to the nose |
| Hockey / curved | — |
| **Denehy's / Bell's** | Named types with defined geometry |

**Permeable spurs are worth noting for Nepal** because they suit the setting: built of **bamboo, timber piles and brushwood**, they are cheap, use local materials, and work by **reducing the velocity and trapping sediment** rather than by resisting the full force of the current — so their failure is gradual rather than catastrophic. Impermeable spurs are stronger but need heavy stone and generate severe **local scour at the nose**, which must be protected by an apron like a guide bank head.

**Revetment (pitching)** armours the bank face directly:

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Dry stone pitching** | Hand-placed stone; cheap, flexible, permeable |
| **Grouted / mortared pitching** | Stronger but **rigid and impermeable** — needs weep holes |
| **Concrete blocks** | Uniform, interlocking types available |
| **Gabion mattress** | Stone in wire mesh; **flexible and permeable** |
| Geotextile bags, sand-cement bags | Where stone is scarce |
| Bio-engineering (vegetation) | Combined with the above at higher levels |

**Three requirements of any revetment**, and neglect of the second or third is the usual cause of failure:

1. **Adequate stone size** to resist the velocity.
2. **A filter layer** (graded stone or geotextile) beneath, or the bank material washes out through the joints and the pitching collapses into the void.
3. **A toe protection or launching apron**, because the current scours the bed at the toe and the pitching then slides down.

**The toe is where revetment fails.** Armouring the visible face while leaving the toe unprotected simply moves the failure to where it cannot be seen until it happens.

**Gabions — the standard Nepali technique**, and the reasons are specifically local:

| Property | Why it matters in Nepal |
|---|---|
| Built from **locally available boulders** | Rivers supply the stone; no transport of manufactured material |
| **No cement, no formwork, no skilled labour** | Can be built by a local workforce in a remote location |
| **FLEXIBLE** | Tolerates **settlement and undermining** without fracturing — it deforms and continues to function, where a rigid wall cracks and fails |
| **PERMEABLE** | **Pore pressure cannot build up behind it**, which is the commonest cause of retaining structure failure on a wet hillside |
| Modular | Can be extended or repaired incrementally |
| Vegetation establishes in the voids | Improves appearance and adds root reinforcement over time |

Its weaknesses are **wire corrosion** (mitigated by galvanising or PVC coating) and **abrasion of the mesh** by boulders rolling in a steep torrent — which is why gabions are less suitable in the steepest boulder reaches, where the bed load itself destroys them.

**Other bank protection techniques:**

| Technique | Use |
|---|---|
| **Bio-engineering** | Grasses, shrubs and bamboo planted on slopes; roots reinforce, foliage intercepts rain, transpiration dries the soil |
| **Cut-off (channel improvement)** | An artificial cut across a meander neck, shortening the course — reduces flood levels but **steepens the slope**, causing degradation |
| Closing bars / bandalling | Closing a subsidiary channel to concentrate flow |
| Dredging | Deepening for navigation or intake depth |

**Bio-engineering deserves the closing emphasis** because it is the technique most suited to Nepal's conditions and most promoted by the Department of Roads and the Department of Water Induced Disaster Management. Its merits are that it uses **local plant species and local labour**, costs a fraction of a structural solution, **strengthens with time** as roots develop (whereas a structure only deteriorates), and addresses both the **water** (interception and transpiration) and the **reinforcement** (roots) aspects of slope failure together.

Its limitations are equally real: it takes **one or two growing seasons to become effective**, so it cannot be relied on for immediate protection; it works on the **shallow** zone that roots reach, not on deep-seated instability; and it needs **protection from grazing** in the establishment period. The standard practice is therefore a **combination** — a structural toe (gabion or masonry) where the current attacks, with bio-engineering on the slope above.

formulas.label: Spur orientation rule
formulas.expression: Pointing UPSTREAM = REPELLING (pushes flow away). Pointing DOWNSTREAM = ATTRACTING (draws flow in).
formulas.note: Repelling is the usual bank-protection choice, set at about 60–75° to the bank.

formulas.label: Lacey normal scour depth
formulas.expression: R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3} ;   or R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3} per unit width
formulas.note: The base value from which all the maximum-scour multipliers are taken.

formulas.label: Maximum scour multipliers on R
formulas.expression: straight guide bank 1.25R ; nose 1.5R ; UPSTREAM CURVED HEAD 2.0–2.75R ; bridge pier nose 2.0R
formulas.note: The upstream curved head takes the deepest scour and is where guide banks usually fail.

formulas.label: Guide bank layout
formulas.expression: upstream length 1.0–1.25 L ; downstream 0.2–0.4 L ; upstream head radius 0.4–0.5 L through 120–145°
formulas.note: The curved heads guide the flow smoothly; a blunt end would cause separation and severe local scour.

formulas.label: Launching apron
formulas.expression: Lay stone on the bed at the toe; it launches down a 2:1 slope, with launched thickness ≈ 1.25 × laid thickness
formulas.note: Avoids founding below the deepest scour — the stone arrives as armour as the bed erodes.

formulas.label: Spur spacing
formulas.expression: 2 to 2.5 times the spur length in a straight reach; closer on a concave bank
formulas.note: A spur field silts up between the spurs, creating a new protected bank line at the spur heads.

formulas.label: Sinuosity
formulas.expression: sinuosity = curved (thalweg) length / straight valley length ;   meandering if > 1.5
formulas.note: The helical current scours the concave OUTER bank and deposits on the convex inner bank.
